#1518. Why Real Madrid and FC Barcelona are no longer recruiting French people

A few years ago, both FC Barcelona and Real Madrid greatly appreciated the French market. Certain players like Aurélien Tchouameni, Eduardo Camavinga or Ferland Mendy are still present in Madrid, while in the 2010s, the Catalan club also enlisted several French players or players playing in Ligue 1. But in recent years, the trend has clearly faded, and if we put aside the market opportunity Ibrahima Konaté or Kylian Mbappé, it is rare to see the two Spanish ogres take an interest in the French market. Of course, there is no doubt that if the possibility of recruiting Michael Olise presented itself, FC Barcelona and especially Real Madrid would jump at it. But it is obvious that in recent years, the two La Liga leaders have turned their backs on French football.

This is not necessarily a talent pool problem, since France continues to produce quality players. First possible explanation: the latest experiences are not really conclusive and therefore do not necessarily invite the two clubs to continue to dig into France. At FC Barcelona, ​​the French and/or Ligue 1 players recently recruited have not been completely satisfactory, on different scales. Malcom, Jean-Clair Todibo, Ousmane Dembélé, Clément Lenglet, Antoine Griezmann and Jules Koundé have some had good moments, but the results are generally bad. At Real Madrid, a similar observation for the players who preceded Karim Benzema or Raphaël Varane. The leaders of the two clubs have therefore perhaps been cooled…

Another explanation, and it is perhaps a little more down to earth than the first: the appearance of new players, and therefore new competitors, on the market. With the appearance of Saudi clubs, and increasingly powerful English clubs, the number of clubs capable of competing with FC Barcelona and Real Madrid has increased considerably. If there could be four or five clubs including Real and Barça on the same player at one time, today there can be around ten. And inevitably this causes colossal inflation in player prices. In 2016, Samuel Umtiti cost FC Barcelona only 25 million euros. Ten years later, there is no doubt that it would have cost at least double.

And it is also valid in the other direction: the power of these new purchasing clubs makes it very complicated to snatch players from them afterwards. FC Barcelona, ​​for example, tried to acquire Eli Junior Kroupi this summer, but Bournemouth demanded a minimum of 100 million euros. A completely prohibitive amount, which Barça cannot or does not want to pay, but which English big names could align themselves with without shaking their chins too much. It must also be said that the recruitment policy of the two clubs has changed: now, we are trying to recruit young players for “correct” sums before they explode and become the stars of tomorrow, a bit like Barça did with Bisiwu or Abdelkarim this summer, and like Real Madrid has been doing for a while too. And players playing in France are already too expensive.

In the case of Barça, we are also obliged to mention this financial crisis which calmed the club’s enthusiasm in the transfer window and which pushed the management to turn, more than was already the case, towards its training center. The decrease in French or Ligue 1 players in the two La Liga giants can also be explained by structural changes. Both, for example, had French managers or advisors internally. Éric Abidal was technical secretary of Barça at the end of the 2010s, and his predecessor, Robert Fernandez, was also an expert in Ligue 1, where he wanted, for example, to enlist Jean Michael Seri. On the Madrid side, Zinédine Zidane, whether as an advisor to Florentino Pérez or as a coach, has also pushed to explore the French market.

Today, Deco and his right-hand man Bojan Krkić, as well as Hansi Flick who also has his say, are not particularly focused on France. At Real Madrid, where Juni Calafat is the main instigator of the transfer windows. Coaches also have decision-making power, although they are not always respected by the hierarchy. The French market is no longer very popular. Calafat is thus more turned towards America, while José Angel Sanchez, general director of the club, is more fond of trying shots in big European clubs. The French are therefore no longer necessarily popular in Spain… until an interesting opportunity presents itself! In the meantime, it’s time for the Clasico!

#1516. Roma set new record for fastest brace at Old Trafford

Roma made history at Old Trafford. Thanks to goals from Soulé and Malen, which came in the first 18 minutes of the match against Manchester United, the Giallorossi set a new record at the English stadium.

Never before had a visiting team managed to score twice so early at Old Trafford in a major European match. Gasperini’s team broke the deadlock in the 11th minute through Soulé, before doubling their lead from the penalty spot seven minutes later through Malen.

This figure applies to all major European competitions played by Manchester United at their home ground, which has never before seen the visiting team score two goals in 17 minutes of play.

This start takes on even greater significance given the teams’ history. Roma had lost all four of their previous meetings at Old Trafford between 2007 and 2021.

Despite the relief caused by this success against the Blues, Maddison’s physical state therefore constitutes the main downside of the London evening.

#1514. Gasperini analyzes loss to Man United: “It teaches us a lot.”

A terrible late defeat condemned Roma to the Champions League.

Leading the way, the Giallorossi saw Manchester United overturn their lead in the final minutes: first a penalty from Bruno Fernandes, then a brace from Matheus Cunha.

The Brazilian first leveled the scoreline with a mistake from Balerdi, then scored the winner in the 86th minute, capping his wild night with a red card in the 91st.

After the match, Gian Piero Gasperini analyzed the painful defeat to Sky Sport, starting with the episode that changed the match’s momentum: “I think it was a different game than the one against Real Madrid,” the Giallorossi coach explained. “There weren’t such obvious signs of a decline, as there were after the penalty, which gave them a great boost.”

No excuses, however, for the inability to stem the Red Devils’ final assault: “There’s no coincidence in the goals we conceded in the comeback; tonight we didn’t have the strength to defend their attackers. It’s natural that you can struggle against Manchester United in the final 15 minutes if they attack like that.”

“They started to press further forward; we had to play differently, taking advantage of long balls. We weren’t able to keep up with them: we should have resorted to a few more tackles, but instead we suffered their momentum, which was amplified by the penalty and the 2-2 incident.”

On managing the right flank and using Lulli in place of the injured Rensch (with Molina left out): “Molina could have stayed in, yes. Rensch started well, then he got injured and I opted for Lulli. But that’s not the reason for the defeat. I think it was a different match, which taught us more than the one against Real Madrid.” He concluded by focusing on the psychological aspect of dealing with the backlash: “There was a bit of disappointment after seeing victory slip away from you at the front. The team perhaps needs to relieve itself of the pressure of a result at all costs.”

#1512. First Anfield victory for 14 years was vindication for Mikel Arteta after Fleetwood humbling. His Arsenal look the finished article - Liverpool were authors of their own downfall, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 13:54 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:32 EDT, 2 November 2026

Five nights ago, 40 miles to the north of Anfield at a remote outpost of English football, Arsenal fell to one of the most humiliating reverses of their long and august history. In the teeth of a gale that blew in off the Irish Sea, they were knocked out of the League Cup by Fleetwood Town, a team 18th in League Two.

They left with their tails between their legs, their teenage prodigy Max Dowman sent off in a melee, their heart questioned, their quality debated, their discipline an issue. Mikel Arteta and his side knew that just a few days later, at the other end of the Fylde Coast and across the Ribble Estuary, they would have to swap running the gauntlet of the Cod Army for the challenge of facing down the roar of the Kop.

They did not shirk it. If Tuesday night was a humbling, their gritty 1-0 victory in an Anfield that was a cauldron once more felt like a significant triumph. It was a defensive masterclass from the champions, an exercise in indomitability. It was their first victory here since 2012 and it took them above Manchester City so that they sit, once more, at the top of the table. Liverpool could not summon a single shot on target.

‘It felt like the end of the world when we were knocked out at Fleetwood,’ Arteta said after this win. ‘You look so silly. I was thinking “How can I lift these players up?” You have to dig deep. This was a mission to win here and it is something that we have not done for 14 years for a variety of reasons. We knew we would have to navigate some difficult moments.’

If Arteta left Fleetwood answering questions about his management of Dowman, he finished this game by striding on to the pitch after the final whistle, pumping his fists in front of the Arsenal fans celebrating in the Anfield Road end, and beating his hand on his chest. This was a vindication for him and his team. Five nights is a long time in football.

He had talked about the harsh realities of this sport after Tuesday’s loss. He had reminded everyone that playing at this level was not like ‘Disneyland’. And this victory was not like Disneyland, either. It was less a theme park and more an assault course. It was rough and it was unforgiving and Arsenal were equal to it.

Liverpool, improving under the management of Andoni Iraola, had been talked up as title contenders ahead of this match on a dank evening on Merseyside where the streets around the ground were decorated with the toothless grimaces of rotting pumpkins on doorsteps. The home team showed exhilarating signs of their re-emergence as an attacking force.

They dominated much of the game, too, but they looked like an emerging team, a team that is still evolving. Arsenal, marshalled imperiously by Declan Rice, looked like the finished article. They created one outstanding chance and Kai Havertz converted it. That was all they needed.

Their defence stayed rock-solid, although there was some puzzlement that Liverpool were not awarded a penalty for Jurrien Timber’s blatant shirt-pull on Alexander Isak. After the interval, Liverpool rarely looked like drawing level.

Kai Havertz gave the Gunners a lead to defend after finishing off a well worked move early on

The German slotted home after Declan Rice fizzed a dangerous ball across the six-yard box

Winning at Anfield was vindication for Mikel Arteta after Arsenal's defeat by Fleetwood Town

The opening had been predictably frenetic. Neither team forged a chance but Trey Nyoni, who has forced his way into the first team with a series of excellent performances in midfield, could have been booked twice inside the first quarter of an hour.

The initial infringement was a nasty tackle on Martin Odegaard inside the first minute where he planted his studs in Odegaard’s ankle. The second was a spiteful tackle on Kai Havertz. Neither received a yellow card, which gave yet more pause for thought about the red card shown to Dowman at Fleetwood, and its aftermath.

Let’s get one thing straight – the criticism of Arteta for his ‘treatment’ of Dowman was absurd. It has come to something when a manager giving a player a hard stare is interpreted by some as a disproportionate response.

Nobody is necessarily hankering after a return to the days of Sir Alex Ferguson’s hairdrier or Joe Kinnear’s rants that broke records for expletives but if a boss is attracting censure because he looked at a player a bit funny, we are in big trouble.

Arteta is not there to indulge Dowman. He is there to coach him and to teach him and to help him grow up in the context of a Premier League football club. His actions in Fleetwood on Tuesday fulfilled his obligations in all of those criteria.

Arsenal survived the initial frenzy here and took the lead after 16 minutes. Liverpool were the authors of their own downfall. They gave the ball away from a goal kick, it was worked to Noni Madueke on the right, and when Madueke fed it to Declan Rice on the overlap, Rice crossed beautifully for Havertz, who touched it home at the back post.

Arsenal nearly returned the favour a minute later when they played themselves into trouble at the back. Bradley Barcola found himself through on David Raya but his first touch let him down and Rice moved across to clear the danger.

Alexis Mac Allister was left with his head in his hands after missing a glorious chance to score

Liverpool's 19-year-old talent Trey Nyoni started the match but was replaced in the second half

Liverpool recovered and began to dominate the game. Barcola’s pace began to cause Arsenal all sorts of problems down their right flank and Liverpool came close to an equaliser when Virgil van Dijk flicked on a corner and Alexander Isak was denied by the brave intervention of Raya.

Arsenal were still threatening on the counter. Christos Tzolis chipped a ball to the back post and, as Liverpool scrambled to clear it, Madueke turned it back across goal. The ball was intended for Havertz, who was unmarked in the middle, but Timber could not get out of the way of it and it bounced off him into touch.

The atmosphere was febrile. Liverpool had three appeals for penalties, first for Timber’s shirt pull on Isak, then for challenges on Alexis Mac Allister and Cody Gakpo, turned down in quick succession. Tempers began to flare on the benches.

The breathlessness of the match was relentless. Florian Wirtz drove a free kick against the face of the crossbar with Raya beaten and then, three minutes before the interval, Mac Allister ran on to a cross from Milos Kerkez and, with the goal at his mercy, directed his free header too high.

Liverpool laid siege to the Arsenal goal after the break but the openings just would not come. Isak blazed high over the bar from an angle, Wirtz had a shot on the turn blocked and then, just before the hour, Dominik Szoboszlai replaced Nyoni and, to more acclaim, Rio Ngumoha came on for Gakpo.

Still Liverpool could not prise Arsenal open. Arsenal began to grow in confidence and threat. The home team were grateful to Jeremy Jacquet for a clearance that prevented Odegaard turning Tzolis’s cross into an open goal, for Van Dijk’s brilliant interception to deny Havertz and, most of all, for a quite magnificent one-handed save from Alisson that diverted a Tzolis shot round the post. It will stand the test of time as one of the saves of the season.

Arsenal put in another excellent defensive display to frustrate and keep Liverpool at bay

Liverpool’s frustration boiled over. Mac Allister was booked for his part in an ugly fracas with Odegaard and Madueke. The stands became a mass of pointing fingers and shouts of protest and anger. Time-wasting and play-acting peppered the match. Liverpool felt the game slipping away in the angst.

Liverpool threw everything at it in the final minutes. Lewis Koumas flung himself at a bouncing ball but could not get enough power on his header, Ngumoha had a shot charged down, Barcola desperately searched for pockets of space but could not find them. There were six minutes of time added on but there was no way through. Arsenal’s defence would not yield.

#1510. The top 10 goalscorers in Europe in the 2020s: Mbappe vs Haaland for top spot, Salah 5th…

Which players have scored the most goals in Europe’s top five leagues in the 2020s?

The 2010s were dominated by Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, but neither are playing in Europe anymore and didn’t get enough goals before they left to stay in the top 10 scorers of the decade.

There are plenty of familiar names in the current top 10 though, with the three leading scorers separated by just three goals.

Here are the 10 players with the most goals across the Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 since the turn of the decade.

Schick knocked ex-Aston Villa striker Ollie Watkins out of the top 10 in October.

He began the 2020s on loan at RB Leipzig from Roma, but went on to find his home at Leverkusen, where’s he’s now closing in on 100 league goals.

Alexander Isak is catching up with him, but Schick is just ahead for now.

After emerging in European football with a prolific spell at Gent, David joined Lille in the summer of 2020.

Over the next five seasons in Ligue 1, 87 goals by the Canada international followed.

He found things a bit tougher in Serie A after joining Juventus in 2025, only scoring six times from 36 league outings so far.

Juventus have sent him on loan to Atletico Madrid for this season and he scored on his La Liga debut.

Arguably the least household name here, Budimir plays for Osasuna and has only ever made it to the play-off rounds of a European competition (the 2023-24 Conference League).

But the 41-cap, seven-goal Croatia international has showcased his reliability in La Liga over the past few seasons, hitting double figures in 2020-21, 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26.

Only Kylian Mbappe and Robert Lewandowski – spoiler alert, but those are two names you’ll be seeing again later – outscored Budimir in La Liga in the 2024-25 season. Then in 2025-26, only Mbappe and the relegated Mallorca frontman Vedat Muriqi scored more.

Now 35, Budimir might not have too much time left at the top level, but is under contract with Osasuna for the rest of the season.

Now 30 years old, Guirassy has played exclusively in France and Germany during his career so far.

He began the 2020s in Ligue 1 with Amiens, but suffered relegation at the end of the 2019-20 season before moving back into the top flight with Rennes.

Whilst with Rennes, he added another 19 Ligue 1 goals to his five from the second half of 2019-20.

A move to Germany with Stuttgart followed in 2022, leading to 39 Bundesliga goals in two years. He came one shy of reaching the same amount from his first two seasons with Borussia Dortmund.

Martinez has been with Inter Milan since the summer of 2018, which means his debut season in Serie A was the only one that didn’t span into any of the 2020s.

It was also the only one in which he has failed to hit double figures of goals. The Argentine striker even enjoyed three consecutive seasons with 20+ goals between 2021-22 and 2023-24, ranking as Serie A’s top scorer for the latter.

Martinez has often played as part of a strike partnership at Inter, but his longevity enables him to outrank colleagues past and present like Romelu Lukaku, Edin Dzeko and Marcus Thuram for goals since the start of the decade.

Salah left Liverpool in the summer for Trabzonspor, marking the end (for now) of his goal-getting in Europe’s top leagues.

He was extraordinary in front of goal after joining Liverpool in 2017, being able to boast 128 Premier League goals in the 2020s alone.

During that time, he claimed two Golden Boots, including from the 2024-25 season when Liverpool won the league.

He should be staying in this top 10 long after his departure from Liverpool thanks to the collection of goals he has already built up.

Lewandowski denied Erling Haaland the chance to win a Golden Boot in the Bundesliga while maintaining outlandish levels of form for Bayern Munich.

Lewandowski then began firing them in for Barcelona, where he moved in 2022. More than 80 La Liga goals followed.

Now at the age of 38, Lewandowski only scored 14 times in the league last season, but has proven wrong anyone who may have doubted his ability to keep scoring regularly at this stage of his career.

The winner of the European Golden Shoe in each of his last two seasons with Bayern, Lewandowski was La Liga’s top scorer in his first with Barcelona.

He is now playing outside of Europe for Chicago Fire in MLS.

Kane has 99 Bundesliga goals to his name from 97 games since joining Bayern Munich in 2023 and was top of this ranking by the end of last season.

Before his spell with Bayern, he enjoyed some prolific seasons towards the end of his time in the Premier League with Tottenham Hotspur, including 30 in his last season.

The 33-year-old is in the final season of his contract with Bayern but is showing no signs of slowing down, even breaking the 60-goal barrier in all competitions last season.

Haaland is still behind Salah in the Premier League scoring chart for the 2020s, but his exploits in the Bundesliga with Borussia Dortmund from the start of the decade place him 50-odd goals above the Liverpool legend here.

Haaland entered Europe’s top five leagues by joining Dortmund in January 2020 and proceeded to score 62 Bundesliga goals from 67 games prior to his move to Manchester City.

The big Norwegian striker was in no mood to slow his scoring rate in England, setting a new Premier League record for most goals in a 38-game season at the first time of asking with 36 (from just 35 appearances).

Haaland shattered through the landmark of 100 Premier League goals during the 2025-26 season and at the age of 26, should still have plenty more goals up his sleeve in the years to come.

Mbappe will most likely be going toe to toe with Haaland over the next few years to finish in top spot.

By the time he left PSG in 2024, Mbappe had become the French club’s all-time record scorer. A move to Real Madrid followed and he went on to score a Pichichi-worthy 31 goals in his first La Liga season.

Mbappe finished with 25 to his name in his second – again being La Liga’s top scorer – which meant he was recently able to pass a half-century of La Liga goals. He will be hungry for more (and silverware) over the coming seasons.

#1507. Can you name Leeds United’s XI from their 4-3 win over Liverpool in 2000?

You probably don’t need to look at the above picture to remember who scored all four goals in Leeds United‘s unforgettable 4-3 victory over Liverpool in November 2000 – but do you know the rest of David O’Leary’s side that day?

It was an individual display destined to be talked about for decades to come by Leeds’ No.9 that afternoon, but the supporting cast wasn’t bad either: this was a side that famously made it all the way to the Champions League semi-finals that season.

“We felt invincible as a club at that time,” said one former midfielder who started for Leeds on that November afternoon. “We attacked every game, we were impossible to play against. We were aggressive and entertaining. We believed we could beat anyone.”

Gerard Houllier’s Liverpool would go on to have the last laugh, winning three trophies in 2000-01 and pipping Leeds to third by just a point. “What happened next was awful,” another Leeds man remembered. “We missed out [on the Champions League] by one point, and from there the finances became a mess.”

But that day undoubtedly belonged to the Yorkshire side. So we’re asking you to name O’Leary’s starting XI. The time to beat from the Leeds fan in the Planet Football office is 00:56.

#1504. Ranking our 10 favourite Champions League comebacks ever after Man Utd 3-2 Roma

Manchester United’s thrilling 3-2 win over Roma was the kind of comeback to be spoken about for years – but it doesn’t quite make our top 10 in Champions League history.

United were two goals down at half-time, before a stirring second-half performance that probably saved Michael Carrick’s job for another week or two.

We’ve ranked our 10 favourite Champions League comebacks of all time, starting in Catalonia with pre-Abramovich Chelsea beginning to pinch themselves…

Finishing 3rd in the Premier League in 1999 was a big deal for Chelsea, who’d only won a single league title in the 1950s.

Getting to the Champions League quarter-finals and beating Barcelona 3-1 in the first leg was dreamland territory.

But Barca were stacked at the turn of the millennium, with Ballon d’Or winner Rivaldo and pre-pig head Luis Figo running the show.

Both Rivaldo and Figo scored at Camp Nou, before Tore Andre Flo pulled one back to edge Chelsea towards the semis.

They almost made it too. There were just eight minutes remaining when Dani took the game to extra-time, before Rivaldo and Patrick Kluivert made it 5-1.

Chelsea would have their revenge 12 years later, but this was a humbling night.

Early 2004 was peak Galactico Madrid, just before it all fell apart.

Figo, Ronaldo, Zidane, Beckham and Raul all featured in their 4-2 quarter-final win over Monaco, a surely unassailable lead to take into the second leg.

But assembling all those Galacticos meant several talented players became collateral damage, including Fernando Morientes. Madrid had loaned him to Monaco for the 2003-04 season, unaware of the potential narrative ramifications.

His goal, alongside two from the wonderful Ludovic Giuly, ensured the Ligue 1 side won the second leg 3-1 and progressed on away goals.

Real Madrid wouldn’t make another Champions League quarter-final for seven years.

Some might call Chelsea’s run to Champions League glory in 2012 the spawniest of all time, but it was really the culmination of years of grit and sheer bloody-mindedness.

The kind of bloody-mindedness that chewed up and spat out Andre Villas-Boas, the young manager unequipped to lead a dressing room containing John Terry, Frank Lampard and Didier Drogba.

One of Villas-Boas’ last matches was a 3-1 defeat at Napoli, seemingly kiboshing their Champions League hopes.

But Roberto Di Matteo took interim charge of the return leg and the players took it upon themselves to save their season.

Drogba, Terry and Lampard all scored to take the tie to extra time at Stamford Bridge, before Branislav Ivanovic’s dramatic winner sent Chelsea through.

If Ousmane Dembele had scored an easy chance at the end of the first leg, Barcelona would’ve taken a four-goal lead to Anfield.

Instead, it was only 3-0 and Jurgen Klopp’s Liverpool smelt blood. Divock Origi began the comeback inside seven minutes, before Andy Robertson ruffled Messi’s head.

Georginio Wijnaldum scored a quickfire double to turn the game into one of *those* nights, before a corner was taken quickly, or something.

Surely the greatest night in Tottenham Hotspur’s recent history – even winning the Europa League couldn’t have provided a rush quite like this.

Especially as the situation looked so unpromising. Ajax had cut a swathe through the Champions League that year, won the first leg in London 1-0 and scored two more in Amsterdam to stretch clear.

Enter Lucas Moura. One of those classic Spurs players who flattered to deceive, Moura scored an incredible hat-trick with the final goal coming in the sixth minute of injury time.

Club legend Glenn Hoddle had suffered a heart attack less than a year before this match. In the BT Sport studio, he remarked how glad he was to have seen it and everyone starting welling up.

Barcelona looked to have this quarter-final tie sewn up in the first leg after Gerard Pique and Luis Suarez added to own goals from Daniele de Rossi and Kostas Manolas.

But Edin Dzeko’s consolation in Spain proved to be crucial as Roma won the second leg by an improbable scoreline of 3-0.

Dzeko put Roma ahead after just six minutes, before a De Rossi penalty and a Manolas header atoned for their Nou Camp mistakes.

The one downside is that Peter Drury’s commentary of Manolas’ clincher went viral and now he’s assaulting our ears on a weekly basis.

The most glorious and life-affirming comeback of all? Probably.

One-nil down as the clock ticked into injury-time, Manchester United had played well within themselves on the biggest stage of all.

Mario Basler’s early goal had given Bayern a lead they’d sat on comfortably all match. Then a corner was taken, Peter Schmeichel’s presence in the box caused mayhem and Teddy Sheringham poked home.

Extra-time beckoned, but United were in the zone. Minutes later, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer had won it, Bayern players collapsed to the floor in despair and football had probably peaked.

Milan started like a greyhound out of the traps, an early Paolo Maldini strike giving the Italians the lead. Brazilian attacking midfielder Kaka then turned on the style and by half-time, he had set up two goals for Hernan Crespo to give Milan a seemingly comfortable 3-0 margin.

But Liverpool boss Rafael Benitez made a big change at the break, bringing on Dietmar Hamann and altering Liverpool’s formation. The decision paid off.

The Reds scored three goals in six wild second-half minutes (Gerrard, Smicer, Alonso), before winning 3-2 in a dramatic penalty shootout that became famous for Jerzy Dudek’s theatrics.

Istanbul has never seen a bigger miracle before or since.

The greatest comeback of all is so iconic that it has its very own title in France and Spain – La Remontada.

PSG took a 4-0 lead to the second leg of this last 16 clash in Spain, only for Luis Suarez to open the scoring for Barcelona in three minutes. Game on.

Barcelona were two goals up at half-time after Layvin Kurzawa’s own goal and Lionel Messi scored a penalty to make it three.

Then, a plot twist. Edinson Cavani hit back to silence Camp Nou, although PSG seemed to go into their shells thereafter.

Needing three goals with two minutes of normal time left, Neymar stepped up to the plate in a way he’d never do again.

The Brazilian scored a free-kick and penalty, before a gorgeous chipped pass found Sergi Roberto to incredibly make it 6-1.

Barcelona became the only team to overturn a foul-goal Champions League deficit. Phowar.

#1503. Roma to pursue Kvernadze in January

Roma continues to monitor Giorgi Kvernadze, the Georgian striker currently playing for Frosinone.

The player was reportedly in the Roman club’s sights last summer and will continue to be monitored ahead of the upcoming transfer window.

This interest could become more concrete in the coming months, especially given the player’s financial terms.

The 2003-born striker is tied to Frosinone by a deal valid until June 30, 2028, but his contract reportedly contains a specific release clause.

The fee required to release the striker is reportedly €4 million, with the option to exercise the option next summer.

This valuation could make the Georgian an attractive prospect for Roma, who are keen to monitor various prospects to strengthen their attacking line.

However, the potential deal would present another financial aspect to consider.

As reported by Gazzetta Regionale, in addition to the €4 million stipulated in the release clause, a significant percentage would need to be considered for the player’s agent.

This detail could impact the overall cost of the deal and the Roma management’s assessment.

Kvernadze’s agent is the same one representing Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, another Georgian talent who has established himself in our Serie A. At the moment, Roma’s interest remains to be monitored, and no official negotiations have been initiated to bring Kvernadze to the capital.

#1502. Arsenal play like the champions they are as title defence starts with a bang

Mentally liberated and physically rested, Arsenal began the new Premier League campaign with a performance befitting champions. Gone are the anxieties of last season, when the title race gnawed away at their minds and bodies. Gone are the pressures of chasing a first Premier League trophy in more than two decades. Arsenal look slick, refreshed and hungry for more.

“Champions of England, we know what we are,” sang the home supporters in this thrashing of promoted Coventry City. The players moved with the same energy and confidence, as they dominated every aspect of this match against Frank Lampard’s side.

There will, of course, be many tougher games than this one over the course of the season. But there can be no doubt that Arsenal are settled and strong. Everywhere Coventry looked, they saw world-class opponents who knew exactly what to do and where to be. This was Coventry’s first Premier League match since 2001 and it was a reminder, as if one was needed, of the size of the gulf between England’s top two divisions. Thankfully for Lampard, his season will not be decided by matches against teams of Arsenal’s quality.

As it was in last weekend’s Community Shield victory over Manchester City, Mikel Arteta’s side purred and flowed in attack. The rejuvenated Martin Odegaard scored again, as did his close friend Kai Havertz. Bukayo Saka also struck, easing any lingering concerns about his fitness. Both Saka and Declan Rice, who endured such draining campaigns last year, looked sharp.

"The champions are on their way!" Kai Havertz sweeps home from the edge of the box to give Arsenal an early lead against Coventry 👏 pic.twitter.com/SNtrMSPkYJ

There was also another promising performance by new signing Christos Tzolis, while midfield dynamo Myles Lewis-Skelly continued where he left off at the end of last season: winning tackles, spinning past opponents and firing up the home crowd. New face Bruno Guimarães, absent through injury for a few days, was certainly not needed here.

“They know how to do it,” Arteta said of his players. “They know what they have to do. There was a lot to like in the performance. The manner we started the game, with such domination, clarity, understanding and flow, it was really impressive. At this level the players have to be decisive. They were certainly decisive today.”

Coventry had attempted to irritate Arsenal with physicality and direct passes, but it never looked likely to work, despite the best efforts of strikers Ellis Sims and Taiwo Awoniyi. They will not be the first team to struggle against Arsenal’s defenders, and this will not be the first occasion in which their goalkeeper Carl Rushworth is kept busy.

“Arsenal were the best team in the league last year and they showed it,” Lampard said. “They played like it. The noise here at the start of the game, it was different. I remember that noise. It’s different to the Championship.”

"They played like champions" 🏆Frank Lampard said Coventry will learn lessons after their 3-0 opening day defeat to Arsenal ❌ pic.twitter.com/wqA2kngUVt

Before this opening match, Arteta had objected to the idea that Arsenal were planning to “defend” their title. Instead, he said, they are going to “attack” the Premier League once again. It was a classic Arteta-ism, but the manager’s meaning was clear: he wants his team to be aggressive, inventive and courageous. Perhaps more so than in the second half of last season, when their defending was a greater strength than their attacking.

If that was a case of Arteta talking the talk, then his players happily followed it up by walking the walk here. Arsenal played with an unmistakable swagger, as if they simply knew there would only be one outcome against a group of Coventry players with limited experience at this level.

The energy of the home supporters, as buoyant as you might expect following last season’s triumph, undoubtedly helped Arsenal. There were none of the nerves that defined the run-in in the spring, with the fans instead in a partying mood from the moment new signing Ezri Konsa was introduced to the Emirates Stadium before kick-off.

The opening goal took only 15 minutes to arrive, as Havertz swept in an accurate finish from Riccardo Calafiori’s low cross. It has been a good summer for Havertz, who missed so much of last season with injury but has found some rhythm over the past few months. Including friendlies and his performances for Germany at the World Cup, this was his 10th goal in his last 17 appearances.

Coventry have invested in some powerful, commanding players this summer, but there were signs that the physical battle was proving difficult for Lampard’s side. Caleb Yirenkyi is their new club-record signing in midfield, but he was brutally thrown to the floor by Lewis-Skelly in the first half.

Saka’s goal was the result of a quick cross by Tzolis, the new £34m winger who has made such an exciting start to his Arsenal career. The Greek forward was the star of the first half, constantly making things happen, and his delivery was diverted into Saka’s path after 23 minutes.

"Saka couldn't miss!"Arsenal are cruising against Coventry as Bukayo Saka fires home from close range 💥 pic.twitter.com/er411Bi1wh

Odegaard showed in the Community Shield that he is in a more confident place than the last campaign, when he constantly battled injuries, and his early-season form continued here. His goal was scruffy, bobbled in off the right foot, but his all-round performance was typically smooth. With two goals in two games, he has already beaten his tally from last season.

"It's a top finish I would say" 😂Martin Odegaard reacts to his goal against Coventry! pic.twitter.com/mciFfZ6Fhx

From there, the game was over. Arsenal could remove Saka, Rice and Odegaard, safe in the knowledge that their work was done. A comfortable night for the champions, and the perfect start.

"How are you going to keep everyone happy? Winning." 🔥Mikel Arteta reveals his secret for keeping his full squad content after Arsenal's 3-0 win against Coventry 👀 pic.twitter.com/IarLijhd6I

"I think we can do even better to be fair" Martin Odegaard reflects on Arsenal's win over Coventry in the first game of the season 💭 pic.twitter.com/nB2YW83VlE

It’s all over in the capital and Arsenal have started their reign as Premier League champions with a confident and assured three-goal victory over newly-promoted Coventry. Havertz, Saka and Odegaard were all on target in a flawless team performance from Arteta’s men. It’s been a tough evening for Lampard’s side, who simply couldn’t handle Arsenal.

FULL-TIME: Arsenal cruise to victory against Coventry on the opening day of the new season! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/ctybTEor9J

There will be four minutes of added time to round this game off. Merino shoots from long range and aims for the bottom corner, but Rushworth dives to his left and makes the stop.

Awoniyi tries to make a run in behind Arsenal’s defence and latch onto Hamer’s pass. The striker is hauled to the ground by Mosquera, who is lucky to escape a booking. The resulting delivery is smacked straight out of play by Torp. That is such a disappointing cross.

Torp swings a cross into Rudoni, who makes a run from deep. Rudoni meets the delivery, but his glancing header is straight at Raya. It’s Coventry’s best chance of the match but they’ve failed to convert it. Arsenal’s clean sheet remains intact.

Arteta makes his fifth and final substitution as Calafiori, who recorded the assist for Arsenal’s opener, is withdrawn for Hincapie.

Lampard responds with his own alteration, bringing Hamer on for Tchaouna.

Coventry are still waiting for their first shot on target this evening. Arsenal are seeing this game out with exemplary professionalism.

Odegaard and Tzolis are the next players to leave the field. Eze and World Cup winner Merino are on as their replacements. Arteta’s substitutions tonight have underlined Arsenal’s tremendous squad depth, and that is without the involvement of both Guimaraes and Konsa.

Lewis-Skelly tries to slide a pinpoint pass through to Calafiori, in an attempt to recreate Arsenal’s opening goal from their Community Shield triumph. It nutmegs Torp, but Rushworth makes a quick dash off his line to collect the ball and eliminate any danger.

Lampard adds some fresh legs and orders a double change. Awoniyi, who makes his Coventry debut, and Rudoni are on, with Simms and Thomas-Asante taken off.

Here come some Arsenal changes. Rice and Saka depart to loud ovations, with Zubimendi and Madueke on to replace them.

Tzolis motors into the Coventry penalty area once again and picks out Havertz, who makes a intelligent run across the six-yard box. Before he can cross or shoot, Thomas sprints over to make an interception.

The visitors then fail to clear a corner and Tzolis slams a low, powerful effort at goal. Rushworth gets down low and spills it, but Thomas is there to hack it away.

Lampard makes the first change of the match for either side as Torp replaces Yirenkyi, whose endured a difficult debut in central midfield for his new side.

Odegaard is enjoying himself out there this evening. Just as he did against Manchester City, he’s playing with such authority, purpose and confidence.

The ball breaks to Tzolis who unleashes a venomous effort at goal. It takes a big deflection and flies out for a corner.

From a Coventry corner, Arsenal counter attack with such intensity and speed. The move ends as Odegaard attempts to find Tzolis with a through ball, but the Norwegian overhits the pass and delayed it too long. The offside flag is then raised against Tzolis.

Van Ewijk attempts to find Simms with a chipped cross towards the back post, but it’s marginally over the striker’s head as Coventry step up their search to pull a goal back.

It’s a nightmare start to the second half for Coventry. Whatever Arteta said to his players at the break has worked wonders.

Lewis-Skelly then shoots from long range and his shot is tipped over the bar by Rushworth.

White overlaps Saka and latches onto the winger’s pass. Saka then tees up Odegaard, who scuffs his close-range effort. Rushworth is wrong-footed and despite getting a glove to it, the ball trickles into the net and Arsenal are cruising.

It's Martin Odegaard... Arsenal have three! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/LrqSSGJWE6

Odegaard has scored some beautiful goals in an Arsenal shirt. That wasn’t one of them. He won’t care, though. Two goals in two games for the Arsenal captain.

Read more about his return to form here: https://www.telegraph.co.uk/football/2026/08/21/odegaard-a-man-possessed-in-bid-to-unlock-arsenal-attack/

We are back under way for the second half. Will Arsenal add more goals to their tally or can Coventry produce a memorable comeback?

It’s been a steep learning curve for the newly-promoted side, who have been overpowered and outclassed by Arsenal’s quality.

Arsenal are in complete control thanks to a commanding first half display against Coventry. Havertz and Saka have the goals, with the reigning Premier League champions on course to claim a routine three points to kickstart their title defence.

Once again, Saka plays a short corner. Odegaard then passes to Rice, who is in acres of space on the edge of the penalty area. The midfielder shoots, but his curling effort drifts narrowly wide of the far post.

There will be two minutes of added time at the end of this half.

The ball bobbles into Tchaouna’s path and the winger tries a very ambitious acrobatic effort from the edge of the box. It had Raya worried for a second, but the effort lands on the roof of the net. That would have been a spectacular goal if it had sneaked in.

Tzolis teases Thomas and works some space before clipping a cross in towards Havertz. The forward doesn’t connect with the header and Coventry scramble it clear.

Odegaard is pulling the strings and slips a delightful pass through to the onrushing White, who finds himself very far forward, but the right back is swiftly closed down by Coventry’s defence as he shoots.

At the other end, Simms does brilliantly to turn Gabriel and win a free kick just outside the box. The Brazilian centre back picks up a yellow card for his troubles.

Coventry are feeling the full effects of the stark difference in levels between Championship and Premier League. Arsenal look streets ahead at the moment.

Christos Tzolis has only played a few games for Arsenal but it’s already easy to see why he registered 29 assists for Club Brugge last season. He has shown on numerous occasions this summer that he is willing to cross the ball as soon as he receives it. No delay, no faff. It worked against Manchester City last weekend and it created Saka’s goal here.

Welcome back to the Premier League, Coventry... It’s been a chastening opening 27 minutes for Lampard’s side.

Yirenkyi then receives a yellow card on his debut for pulling Lewis-Skelly’s shirt.

Rice strides through midfield and plays a one-two with Odegaard. The English midfielder tees up Tzolis, whose fires a cross into the corridor of uncertainty. Rushworth parries it into the danger zone, gifting an unmarked Saka a simple finish from close range. What a start for the champions!

"Saka couldn't miss!"Arsenal are cruising against Coventry as Bukayo Saka fires home from close range 💥 pic.twitter.com/er411Bi1wh

Arsenal are purring and oozing confidence. Coventry need to be careful and must stay in this game. They cannot allow Arsenal to get a second and run away with this.

Coventry had started well but their first error in defence was ruthlessly punished. That’s Havertz’s 10th goal in his last 17 matches for club and country (including pre-season friendlies). After such an injury-disrupted campaign last year, he’s had a very good summer.

Van Ewijk fails to clear his lines and he’s closed down by Tzolis. The ball ricochets into Calafiori’s path and the left back picks out Havertz with a low cross.

The German sweeps a composed shot into the bottom corner. It’s such a cultured finish and Arsenal begin their defence of the Premier League with a 1-0 lead after 15 minutes.

"The champions are on their way!" Kai Havertz sweeps home from the edge of the box to give Arsenal an early lead against Coventry 👏 pic.twitter.com/SNtrMSPkYJ

Some steady possession for Coventry, who are looking to take the sting and excitement out of the game while also calming the buoyant Arsenal fans down.

Tzolis pops up on the right wing and latches onto Rice’s pass. The attacker then delivers a first-time cross into the box which finds Saka, whose half-volley is blocked by Amenda.

Arsenal then work a short corner that ends with White teeing up Tzolis, but his low strike is smothered by Coventry’s defence. Tzolis has certainly made a lively start, and unsurprisingly, Arsenal’s set pieces are causing some early problems.

Tzolis looks dangerous as he dribbles at Van Ewijk, before cutting inside and unleashing a powerful shot. However, his effort is high and wide. Nevertheless, it’s positive play from Arsenal’s new signing.

Following that Coventry corner, the Premier League holders have monopolised the possession in the early minutes. Chants of ‘Champions of England, we know what we are’ ring around the stadium thanks to the home support, who are in full voice.

Coventry get us under way and the newly-promoted side have won an early corner, which is comfortably dealt with by Arsenal’s defence.

The atmosphere at the Emirates is electric. Can Arsenal flex their title-winning credentials once again or will Coventry cause an almighty upset?

New Arsenal signing Ezri Konsa has been presented on the pitch, with both sets of players set to follow him any moment now.

The 2026-27 season is just minutes away from kicking off.

Coventry have recruited some powerful, aggressive players this summer. They will be looking to frustrate Arsenal by shutting down the spaces around their penalty area, and they will certainly be competitive at set-pieces.

Meanwhile, the Arsenal fans have just had their first glimpse of Ezri Konsa in the club’s shirt. The new signing walked out onto the pitch to wave to the supporters.

With just over five minutes until the 2026-27 Premier League season starts, here are tonight’s teams in full...

Arsenal: Raya, White, Mosquera, Gabriel, Calafiori, Odegaard, Rice, Lewis-Skelly, Saka, Havertz, Tzolis.

Subs: Arrizabalaga, Hincapie, Eze, Gyokeres, Madueke, Nwaneri, Merino, Zubimendi, Dowman.

Coventry: Rushworth, van Ewijk, Thomas, Amenda, Dasilva, Onyeka, Yirenkyi, Grimes, Thomas-Asante, Simms, Tchaouna.

Subs: Wilson, Rudoni, Sakamoto, Awoniyi, Kitching, Latibeaudiere, Eccles, Overgaard, Hamer.

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Arsenal boss said: “He had a slight tension in his groin. He hasn’t done a pre-season, he only had four or five days before that [Man City] game. We have to take a lot of new stuff for him as well. We need to take it bit by bit.”

Another game, another snub for Gabriel Martinelli. As was the case against Manchester City in last weekend’s Community Shield, the Brazilian isn’t even on the bench tonight. It’s quite clear what’s going on here: Arsenal need to make sales and he is an obvious candidate to depart. It’s not particularly pleasant, though, and you can’t help but feel for a player who has been so important to this club over the last seven years.

Martinelli has made it clear he does not want to move to Galatasary, who made an offer recently. Will a more suitable club come forward for him? We’ll find out in the coming days.

In two full seasons at Coventry between 2021 and 2023, Viktor Gyokeres scored 40 goals in 97 games for Coventry, and was part of the side that lost on penalties to Luton Town in the Championship play-off final to Luton Town.

If Coventry had won that game, would Gyokeres still be wearing a sky blue shirt instead of joining Sporting CP and then Arsenal, who knows...

The striker will have to wait to get onto the pitch against his former team, with Mikel Arteta choosing Kai Havertz to lead the line.

Odegaard comes into the new Premier League season, which begins when Arsenal host Coventry City on Friday night, with a point to prove. That may sound unusual, given his new-found status as a title-winning captain, but last year was a strange one for the 27-year-old. The club’s most successful campaign of his time at Arsenal was also the most frustrating one for Odegaard as an individual.

Last season, Arsenal clinched a much-anticipated Premier League title for the first time in 22 years and are the favourites to lift the trophy for a second successive season. Mikel Arteta’s side have recently claimed the Community Shield and look like they mean business.

Arsenal are clearly not resting on their laurels in their bid to win another top-flight title, having strengthened their squad this summer with the signings of Bruno Guimarães, Christos Tzolis and Ezri Konsa.

Arteta looks raring to go and ready to mount another title charge.

"Everything has to start with me" 💪Mikel Arteta says Arsenal are ready for the new Premier League season 💥 pic.twitter.com/rsUcs7ot7T

After last season’s Championship by a whopping 95 points under Frank Lampard’s management, Coventry head into their first Premier League campaign since suffering relegation from the competition in 2001.

Coventry were playing in the fourth tier as recently as 2017, so lining up against the Premier League holders is a full-circle moment for the club and supporters that is richly deserved.

"I loved it, I loved driving here, feeling the atmosphere, the fans" Frank Lampard on what tonight means for him and Coventry 😍Watch live here: https://t.co/0AejI4B8dF pic.twitter.com/077Bga2Z4W

On Friday night, at the home of champions Arsenal, Coventry officially begin a new chapter back in the Premier League and expectations will be high. The man responsible for that tidal wave of optimism is Lampard, their promotion hero.

He has proved a transformative appointment since arriving in November 2024, and the former England and Chelsea captain is relishing the chance to rattle some cages.

His return is a feel-good story and Lampard has a point to prove. He admits that the desire to upset his detractors drives him on. “I’ve got experience of the Premier League and hopefully I can get that across to the players,” he said.

“The club has been out of this division for 25 years so of course it’s exciting. We want to challenge and we want to do well. I’m pleased that we’re here and you want to work at the top. We’re very focused on the job.”

Arsenal ruined Enzo Maresca’s first competitive outing as Man City’s new manager in the club’s first match without Pep Guardiola. It was one-way traffic as Arsenal cruised to a resounding 3-0 win to lift the Community Shield in Cardiff.

Riccardo Calafiori opened the scoring just 23 seconds after he was brilliantly played in by Myles Lewis-Skelly’s defence-splitting pass. Arsenal doubled their lead before the half-hour mark through Kai Havertz’s close-range header and Martin Odegaard added a sumptuously taken third shortly after the interval.

The Premier League holders were in a ruthless mood and completely overran their opponents. Christos Tzolis grabbed two assists out on the left wing, Bruno Guimarães produced a typically commanding performance in the first half and Odegaard controlled proceedings with his creativity.

It was an early taste of silverware for Mikel Arteta’s men, who are the overwhelming favourites to retain their Premier League crown.

"I'm really pleased, that's a really good team" Ian Wright is happy with the Arsenal starting XI to face Coventry, do you agree? 💬 Watch live: https://t.co/0AejI4B8dF pic.twitter.com/IUBlMS963w

New signings Aurele Amenda, Loum Tchaouna and Caleb Yirenkyi all start and make their Coventry debuts this evening.

Carl Rushworth and Frank Onyeka also begin from the outset after making their moves permanent following successful loans last season.

Your City tonight. 📋 pic.twitter.com/V0nzaemLYF

As Sam Dean confirmed earlier on, Bruno Guimaraes is absent from the squad. The Brazilian was subbed off at half-time in the dominant Community Shield victory over Manchester City with a thigh issue.

Both Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka start after being used off the bench in the Community Shield last weekend, with Guimaraes and Noni Madueke dropping to the bench.

🔴 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 ⚪️Your Premier League opening day XI ✊🤝 Presented by @deel pic.twitter.com/yRf2BEs3BA

To soften the blow of Bruno Guimaraes’ absence from tonight’s squad due to injury, the Premier League holders can rejoice over the signing of Ezri Konsa from Aston Villa for over £50m.

The centre back has penned a four-year deal with the option of a further year.

Speaking to Arsenal’s official website, Sporting Director Andrea Berta said: “Ezri is a defender of high quality, whose athleticism, composure and tactical intelligence have established him as one of the Premier League’s most consistent performers.

“Being comfortable in both central defence and at right-back, Ezri will bring valuable versatility to our squad while maintaining the high defensive standards which are fundamental to our challenge of winning major trophies.”

Konsa will play no role in tonight’s encounter, having only completed the move earlier in the day.

Reinforcing the backline ✍️ pic.twitter.com/deYQhZcmOy

Good evening and welcome to the Emirates Stadium, where the Premier League champions begin the defence of their title. Or, as Mikel Arteta prefers to put it, their “attack” on a new season. A classic Arteta-ism.

The assault starts tonight against Coventry City but our understanding is that Arsenal will be without new £75m midfielder Bruno Guimaraes. We believe the Brazilian has picked up an injury, and it’s not currently clear how severe it might be. Clearly, this is a blow for Arteta. But they should still have enough to get past promoted Coventry… shouldn’t they? We’ll find out soon enough.

Meanwhile, Arteta has said he and his players should relish being Premier League title favourites and the role of the hunted rather than the hunter.

“In the last three seasons, at some point we were first and at some point we were chasing. And you never know what is better,” Arteta said. “But if you give me the choice, I want to be first. I want to be hunted, and I want to be in control of our future, rather than depending on somebody else.”

Arteta called on his players to retain the hunger they had last season.

“We start from scratch, from zero, and we’re going to have to prove we are at the level to go back to that position again,” he said. “We need to show that desire and the ambition to be better than what we were last season, a month ago, a week ago.”

This is Coventry’s first Premier League campaign since they suffered relegation in 2000-01, and they were led to the Championship title by Frank Lampard. They scored the most goals in the Championship and conceded the fewest, and could face one of their former players tonight in Viktor Gyokeres.

#1501. Ranking the 10 right-backs in world football right now: Who are the closest to matching Achraf Hakimi?

The title of world’s best right-back isn’t up for much debate, but the race for the remaining places is fiercely contested.

Europe’s elite are packed with top-class options, with stars from Arsenal, Barcelona, Tottenham, Chelsea and Real Madrid among the standouts. Some thrive as attacking outlets, others excel defensively, while the very best manage to do both.

Here’s our ranking of the 10 best right-backs in world football right now.

There’s something of a Reece James mk.II about Livramento.

Another outstanding Chelsea academy graduate blessed with everything he needs to reach the top, but one whose progress has unfortunately been stunted by injuries.

He’s barely featured this season, with the usual injury issues making it difficult to judge where he’s currently at. But with Newcastle struggling under Matthias Jaissle, the manager could desperately do with a player of Livramento’s quality fit and available.

A safe bet to be England’s starting right-back at the next Euros, provided he can stay on the pitch.

The Italy youth international is already a regular in the transfer gossip columns, but another season of development at Brentford should do him the world of good before the inevitable leap to a Champions League club.

Kayode’s Rory Delap-esque long throws are a fun bonus, but don’t let them overshadow how he already looks like one of the most promising young right-backs in Europe.

Having never managed more than three assists in a league campaign before, Ryerson suddenly turned into one of Europe’s most productive full-backs in the latter half of last season.

The Norwegian ended the 2025-26 Bundesliga season with an outrageous tally of 15 assists, which included four in one game against Mainz.

We’ve seen a reversion to the mean this season, with zero assists to his name, but he’s been solid enough as Dortmund have started in fine fettle, going toe-to-toe with Bayern Munich.

Three La Liga titles. A permanent fixture for France. Another World Cup run deep into the knockout stages. The CV is unquestionable.

But actually watch him play, rather than read his Wikipedia career summary, and you’ll come away with a different impression. Kounde hasn’t looked as assured over the past couple of years as he did at his peak.

He’s still a decent enough right-back, but there are too many switch-offs and untidy moments. Barcelona’s high line is unforgiving, but we still expect more from a player of his ability.

We’re not writing him off, but it’s been a long while since we’ve looked at Kounde and thought of him as one of the outstanding players in his position.

La Masia does it again. Espart has enjoyed an outstanding breakthrough campaign, establishing himself as Hansi Flick’s best right-back and putting Kounde’s place under genuine pressure.

He’s a wonderfully versatile teenager, capable of filling several roles and looking comfortable wherever he’s deployed. His future might ultimately lie further forward in midfield, but for now he’s making the right-back position his own.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is nowhere to be seen in our top 10 right-backs. Some drop-off for a player who boldly stated his ambitions of winning a Ballon d’Or.

We’ve also kicked Denzel Dumfries out of this list for Valverde, who would’ve featured pretty prominently in a midfielders ranking in his prime a couple of years back.

The Los Blancos captain might be playing there reluctantly, which caused a bit of a stir last season, but we find ourselves agreeing with Jose Mourinho.

“It hurts me. Our squad planning was to have two players in each position, and now I’m playing a third guy in their place (Valverde), and that really makes me sad,” the Real Madrid manager said recently.

“In this very specific situation, I think it’s better for the team to play Fede there. I consider Fede a more offensive RB than the other two right now.

“We explained this situation to Trent and Dumfries, and they both accepted it as they understood it’s what best for the team right now.”

READ: Ranking the 10 best midfielders in world football: Rodri, Rice, Vitinha…

Having Porro as high as fourth in this list would’ve felt like a sick joke a few months back.

This is a fella who featured prominently for a Tottenham side that finished 17th in successive Premier League campaigns, with a disastrous defensive record in both.

But this is the danger of judging an individual in a collective context. Stick him in a functional set-up – i.e. Luis de la Fuente’s Spain – and Porro’s quality immediately becomes clear.

He looked every inch the complete right-back at the World Cup: positionally intelligent, defensively assured and a constant threat going forward.

Porro has spent most of this season sidelined, but he’s returning just as Roberto De Zerbi’s side are turning a corner. Watch this space.

There’s an argument that James is too versatile for his own good.

The Chelsea captain can excel in midfield, but that only underlines what an exceptional footballer he is. His best position remains right-back, where few can match his blend of all-round qualities.

Fitness has prevented James from climbing higher. He managed more minutes last season but still missed a significant spell, including much of the World Cup.

Add in Chelsea’s tactical instability and scattergun squad building, and it’s easy to forget just how good he is. If availability wasn’t an issue, and he was playing in a proper team, he’d be challenging for the top two.

Perhaps we’ll see him at his very best under Xabi Alonso this season. But those injury setbacks remain a curse.

Timber’s paltry return in terms of goals and assists is why he isn’t close to the top spot here. He’s never going to be spoken about in the same breath as a Dani Alves or a Cafu.

But with elite attack-minded right-backs in short supply, Timber’s defensive excellence is enough to earn him second place.

Arguably the best one-on-one defender in world football, he was instrumental in Arsenal’s Premier League triumph and coming within a penalty shootout of Champions League glory.

“ACHRAF HAKIMI. BEST RB IN THE WORLD. GOOD NIGHT GUYS. 👋🏽” posted Kylian Mbappe during the 2022 AFCON.

We’ve got a whole series of these rankings. Strikers. Wingers. Centre-backs. In no other position was the No.1 spot so cut and dried.

Hakimi is head and shoulders above the rest. A back-to-back Champions League winner and a key part of Morocco becoming a genuine force in international football.

#1500. Gabriel and Mac Allister's cheating is not just embarrassing, it's malevolent and wicked... players need the threat of red cards for such dishonesty and - if that fails - punishments after review, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 18:05 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:37 EDT, 2 November 2026

Football’s lawmakers like to meddle. The problem is they do it in areas that tend not to need any meddling. Like around handball and offside and other places that were doing just fine as they were.

So here’s a tip for the meddlers at the International Football Association Board. Meddle somewhere that needs it. Meddle in a way that would be meaningful and important and in a way that would actually help the game.

Please meddle with cheating. Please do something that would spare us from the embarrassment of grown men behaving like children in a bid to get other players booked and sent off. Yes, please meddle there.

Because football at the top level really needs it.

It needs a route through which players such as Alexis Mac Allister and Gabriel Magalhaes can be properly punished, shamed and embarrassed for what they did during Sunday’s otherwise fabulous Premier League game between Liverpool and Arsenal at Anfield.

It needs a deterrent. It needs greater power to match referees and greater leeway for retrospective punishment.

Alexis Mac Allister drops to the floor holding his face after his forehead is slightly brushed

The Liverpool man tried to get Noni Madueke sent off during Arsenal's 1-0 victory at Anfield

In a way, it is handy that there was one from each team this time. That way, we can be spared the usual accusations of bias that tend to come when footballers are called out for their sins.

Here, live on TV, Gabriel and Mac Allister were both as bad as each other. One in each half, clear as day.

Arsenal defender Gabriel was poked in the chest early on by Aleksandar Isak and went down holding his face. Then, much later, Liverpool’s Mac Allister was brushed by the forehead of Noni Madueke and did likewise.

Neither fooled referee Andy Madley. Both were told to get up and get on with the game. On TV, Sky Sports analysts Gary Neville and Jamie Carragher didn’t hold back.

‘Embarrassing’ was the word they both chose. Neville to describe Gabriel and Carragher as a way of calling out Mac Allister.

But this type of chicanery is more than that. We see it from lots of players and we see it all the time. It’s not just embarrassing. It goes much deeper. It’s malevolent. It’s low. It’s pre-meditated. It’s wicked.

Short of dark subjects such as spitting and leg-breaking tackles, I can’t think of much worse things on a football field than pretending to have a head or facial injury when you actually haven’t.

So where IFAB need to get involved – where they need to ‘meddle’ – is simple. They must increase football’s powers to punish.

On the field and in the moment, referees can issue yellow cards for simulation and for cheating. Players can be booked for exaggerating contact (Mac Allister) or pretending contact has been made with a certain area of the body when it hasn’t (Gabriel).

Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhaes performed a similar act of cheating in the first half

The Brazilian fell down clutching his face after Alexander Isak brushed his neck and chest

But why is there no power – at least in occasional and exceptional circumstances - to issue a red card?

Gabriel and Mac Allister appeared to be trying to get their opponents sent off. Would they do it if they knew the match referee at least had the option of showing them the red card instead?

Retrospectively, meanwhile, we need greater leeway for action.

Under a law passed a decade ago, a player can theoretically be banned by a review panel for two-games for ‘successful deception of a match official’. However the reality is that the initiative has largely been superseded by VAR and was only really used for players diving to try and win penalties anyway.

In terms of the nonsense we witnessed at Anfield on Sunday – and indeed see on a reasonably regular basis around the country – there is very little recourse once the game is over so once again a possible deterrent has been removed from the equation.

Cheating of this nature currently looks and feels like a risk worth taking and that is what must change.

Alexander Isak was not given a penalty despite being blatantly pulled back by Jurrien Timber

Here, it was interesting to hear Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola suggest afterwards that he must start telling his players to go down under contact. He was talking about Isak’s refusal to buckle under a clear penalty area shirt tug from Jurrien Timber.

That’s an important issue, too. Players should not be punished for their honesty. A foul is a foul, regardless of the reaction. VAR should have awarded a penalty.

But here on an otherwise fine day for the Premier League, another known and rather ugly blot on the landscape grew larger.

The threat of red cards for cheating and – if that fails - punishments handed down by review. That’s the kind of meddling we should all be on board with.

#1498. Ranking the 10 left-backs in world football right now: Mendes, Cucurella, Calafiori…

Left-backs at Arsenal, PSG, Real Madrid, Inter, Manchester City and Bayern Munich can all be considered to be among the standouts in their position across world football right now.

Whether it’s locking down elite wingers, inverting into midfield or providing width in attack, these are the players doing it better than anyone else.

Here’s our ranking of the 10 best left-backs in world football at this moment in time.

Probably not even the best left/centre-back hybrid at his club, which is more of a statement of the scary defensive depth that Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal are blessed with.

The rugged Ecuadorian is unlikely to ever challenge the assists charts, but he’s remarkably sturdy and reliable.

Few full-backs have ever been as exhilarating as Alphonso Davies in full flight.

We will never forget that electric performance against Barcelona, and desperately hope that isn’t as good as it gets. It’d be a minor footballing tragedy if Davies peaked as a teenager.

Unfortunately, we’re starting to fear that might be the reality. Injuries have certainly disrupted Davies’ progress, and he hasn’t quite looked the same electric presence we’ve come to expect.

There have, however, been enough encouraging signs this season to suggest there’s still plenty of life in him.

Regular watchers of the Bundesliga will tell you how solid Brown is. For everyone else, they discovered him at the World Cup – one of very few individuals to escape from Germany’s desperately disappointing campaign with any credit in the bank.

You can see why Bayern moved quickly to secure his signature. Given Davies’ aforementioned struggles, it was a no-brainer of a signing – the Bavarians foodchaining their domestic competition yet again.

He’s not exactly been a revelation since arriving at the Allianz Arena, but has slotted into Vincent Kompany’s side comfortably enough, contributing a goal and two assists in his first eight Bundesliga appearances. There’s plenty more to come, and if he continues developing under the Belgian, there’s no reason why he can’t establish himself among the very best in his position.

The Manchester City academy graduate has the talent and potential to be challenging for the top end of this list, but things haven’t quite clicked under Enzo Maresca just yet.

He’s been in and out of the team during an underwhelming start to life under the new manager, making it difficult to build any real momentum. We’ve still favoured O’Reilly over Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly, having seen considerably more of him at left-back over the past year.

As with Lewis-Skelly, we suspect O’Reilly’s long-term future might lie in midfield. He certainly possesses the technical skill set to make it happen. But there’s still plenty more work to do before he fulfils his considerable potential.

Manchester United were desperate to sign Hall last summer, but Newcastle stood firm. Given the bin fire they’ve subsequently continued to serve up at Old Trafford, he might consider himself fortunate.

That’s not to say Hall isn’t an excellent young footballer. He’s just no magician, and even his considerable talent hasn’t been enough to elevate Matthias Jaissle’s struggling Newcastle side.

One of those players who could look absolutely sensational in a properly functioning team. We’re still backing him to get there.

Grimaldo played a grand total of zero minutes in Spain’s World Cup triumph.

The former Bayer Leverkusen wingback spoke of his eagerness to play his part, but he’s a bit unfortunate that one of the few better players in his position across world football shares his nationality.

Grimaldo has made an outstanding start to life at Atletico Madrid, quickly establishing himself as one of Diego Simeone’s key players. He’s been a standout performer as Atleti look to challenge Barcelona and Real Madrid for the La Liga title.

Not quite to the same extent as some of the prior names in this list, but we’re still left with a sense that Calafiori’s lack of durability costs him a little.

The Italian heartthrob played a decent amount of football last season – 36 appearances and over 2000 minutes in all competitions – but he still missed vast swathes of Arsenal’s quadruple chase, including much of the Premier League run-in and latter stages of the Champions League knockouts.

Calafiori undoubtedly possesses the ability – particularly on the defensive side of his game – to challenge at the top end of this ranking, and he’s showing it more consistently this season. He’s also offering plenty going forward, an aspect of his game that’s becoming increasingly prominent.

Dimarco suffered such a colossal mare in Inter’s 2025 Champions League final shellacking at the hands of PSG that it’s difficult to imagine his reputation ever fully recovering.

But every footballer has their off days, and if you take that out of the equation and Di Marco’s track record is outstanding. Two Scudetti, three Coppa Italia, runs to two Champions League finals, twice being included in the Serie A Team of the Season.

And it’s not just pedigree. Last season was probably his best yet, having notched seven goals and 17 – yes, seventeen – assists as Inter waltzed to the title. He was deservedly named Serie A’s MVP – how often has that ever happened to a full-back in a top European league?

Inter have had an up-and-down start to this campaign, but he remains one of their best and most important players. Badly missed in the recent Milan derby defeat.

Positionally astute, bit of a sh*thouse, decent enough going forward but never at the expense of his defensive duties. Real Madrid have basically signed Jose Mourinho’s idea of the perfect left-back.

Best of all, he’s a big game player. Three summers in a row he’s shone on the big stage. The European Championship. The Club World Cup. The World Cup. Across all three finals, he didn’t put a foot wrong. He was far too good to be playing in a Chelsea side so dysfunctional.

Cucurella looked exposed and out of sorts during the unconvincing early weeks of Jose Mourinho’s reign, struggling badly in defeat to Atletico Madrid. But he’s grown into the campaign as the new manager has tweaked his way towards a more functional set-up.

He was outstanding in the recent El Clasico win, effectively shutting down Spain team-mate Lamine Yamal. Yan Diomande helping out makes a big difference, and Cucurella will probably be hoping Vini Jr doesn’t reclaim his place any time soon.

The case isn’t quite as cut and dried as with Achraf Hakimi on the opposite flank, but it was nevertheless a pretty easy decision.

Mendes and Hakimi have been integral to Luis Enrique’s PSG winning back-to-back Champions Leagues.

Their defensive ability is the starting point, with both excelling in one-on-one duels, but they are far from limited when it comes to supporting the attack. That all-round skill set forms one of the pillars of a remarkably effective set-up.
